html:
Unit circle — special angles

Slider position 0 selects the 0°/360° point; “Clear selection” returns the figure to the plain diagram. Hover a dot: its reference-angle partners are ringed. Click a dot: the radius becomes a right triangle whose legs are cos θ (blue) and sin θ (green).

plan.contextChunk: This figure consists of one large unit circle annotated with the standard special angles and the coordinates of their terminal points. A heavy black circle is centered on thin horizontal and vertical axes, and sixteen straight radii run from the center out to filled dots placed every 30 or 45 degrees around the circumference. Each dot carries an external label in two colors: the angle written in degrees and then in radians in red, followed by the point's (x, y) coordinates in black. Reading counterclockwise from the right, the labels begin 0 degrees, 0, (1, 0), with 360 degrees, 2pi, (1, 0) printed directly beneath it, then 30 degrees, pi/6, (sqrt(3)/2, 1/2); 45 degrees, pi/4, (sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(2)/2); 60 degrees, pi/3, (1/2, sqrt(3)/2); and 90 degrees, pi/2, (0, 1) at the top. The second quadrant continues with 120, 135, and 150 degrees and closes at 180 degrees, pi, (-1, 0); the third runs 210, 225, and 240 degrees to 270 degrees, 3pi/2, (0, -1); and the fourth returns through 300 and 315 degrees to 330 degrees, 11pi/6, (sqrt(3)/2, -1/2). The symmetric placement is the point of the layout, since the same three magnitudes 1/2, sqrt(2)/2, and sqrt(3)/2 recur in every quadrant with only their signs changing. Gathering all the major angles on one circle lets values outside the first quadrant be recovered by reflection rather than recomputed.

interactionPlan.concept: Every special angle on the unit circle has a terminal point whose coordinates are (cos θ, sin θ), and the same three magnitudes — 1/2, √2/2, √3/2 — repeat in all four quadrants with only the signs changing.
elements: Heavy black unit circle centered at origin
Thin horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis through the center, with arrowheads at ±1 on each axis
Sixteen straight radii from center to the circumference at every 30° and 45°
Sixteen filled black dots on the circumference at 0/360, 30, 45, 60, 90, 120, 135, 150, 180, 210, 225, 240, 270, 300, 315, 330 degrees
Red degree labels for each point (0°, 30°, 45°, ... 330°, plus 360° beneath 0°)
Red radian labels as fractions of π (0, π/6, π/4, π/3, π/2, 2π/3, 3π/4, 5π/6, π, 7π/6, 5π/4, 4π/3, 3π/2, 5π/3, 7π/4, 11π/6, 2π)
Black coordinate labels in exact radical form, e.g. (√3/2, 1/2), (√2/2, √2/2), (1/2, √3/2), (0, 1), (-1, 0), (0, -1)
Dual label at the right: 0°, 0, (1,0) with 360°, 2π, (1,0) printed directly beneath
Highlight ring/outline used to mark symmetric points sharing a reference angle (hover state)
Dashed horizontal and vertical projection segments from a selected point down to the axes (click state)
Cosine leg drawn along the x-axis and sine leg drawn vertically, colored differently, forming a right triangle with the radius
Readout annotation box showing θ, cos θ, sin θ for the selected angle
Reference-angle arc annotation at the origin for the selected point
Legend/mode indicator for the active label set

interactions.teaches: Each terminal point carries three equivalent names (degrees, radians, coordinates), and the points sharing its reference angle in the other quadrants have the same coordinate magnitudes with flipped signs.
The x-coordinate of the terminal point IS cos θ and the y-coordinate IS sin θ, read off as the legs of the right triangle formed by the radius.

interactions.label: Label set
interactions.teaches: Degree measure, radian measure, and the coordinate pair are three descriptions of one fixed point, so any one of them can be recalled from the others.

interactions.label: Angle θ (degrees, snaps to special angles)
interactions.teaches: Sweeping counterclockwise shows the coordinates changing sign quadrant by quadrant while the magnitudes cycle through 1/2, √2/2, √3/2 and back.

demo_steps.title: The whole circle at once
demo_steps.narration: All sixteen special angles appear with their degree measure, radian measure, and exact coordinates. Notice the radii are evenly spaced every 30° or 45°.

demo_steps.title: Strip to radians
demo_steps.narration: Hiding the degrees and coordinates leaves only the radian measures, so you can rehearse the π/6, π/4, π/3 families without the clutter.

demo_steps.title: Coordinates are cosine and sine
demo_steps.narration: Select 30°: dashed projections drop to the axes and the radius becomes the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs read √3/2 across and 1/2 up — exactly (cos 30°, sin 30°).

demo_steps.title: Reflect into the second quadrant
demo_steps.narration: Move to 150°. Same reference angle of 30°, same magnitudes, but the x-coordinate is now negative: (-√3/2, 1/2).

demo_steps.title: Both coordinates negative
demo_steps.narration: At 210° the reflection continues into the third quadrant and both projections point in the negative direction: (-√3/2, -1/2).

demo_steps.title: The 45° family
demo_steps.narration: Jump to 225°, where the triangle is isosceles and both coordinates share the magnitude √2/2 — the tell-tale signature of every 45° multiple.

demo_steps.title: Back to the start
demo_steps.narration: Sweeping past 330° returns to the point (1, 0), which is both 0 and 2π — the circle closes and the values repeat.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: You never memorize sixty-four numbers: you memorize three magnitudes (1/2, √2/2, √3/2) for the first quadrant and recover every other special angle by reflecting the point and fixing the signs.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Centered square layout: one large heavy-stroke black circle on thin black axes with small arrowheads at ±1. Sixteen thin radii from the origin to filled black dots every 30°/45°. Each dot's label sits outside the circle, radially aligned with its point: red degree measure, then red radian measure as a stacked fraction of π, then black exact coordinates in parentheses with radicals. On the right, the 0°/0/(1,0) label has 360°/2π/(1,0) directly beneath it. Interaction styling: hovering a dot brightens its own label and draws thin colored outline rings around the 1–3 other dots sharing the same reference angle. Clicking a radius thickens it, draws a dashed vertical segment from the point to the x-axis and a dashed horizontal segment to the y-axis, colors the cosine leg (along x) one hue and the sine leg (vertical) another, shades the small reference-angle arc at the origin, and shows a readout box in a corner with θ in both measures plus cos θ and sin θ in exact form. Label-mode toggle fades out the unselected label categories while all dots and radii stay fixed, emphasizing that the geometry is unchanged. Keep the red/black two-color scheme of the original; use a distinct accent color (e.g. blue for cosine, green for sine) only for interactive overlays.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Hover for each terminal point: the learner points at a dot on the circle, its degree measure, radian measure, and coordinate label brighten while symmetric points with the same reference angle are outlined, making the repeated magnitudes and quadrant sign changes clear.
- Click for component projections: the learner clicks an angle ray, horizontal and vertical projection segments drop to the axes and the coordinate pair is rebuilt as (cos theta, sin theta), connecting the unit-circle point to the two trigonometric values.
- Toggle between degree, radian, and coordinate label modes: the learner switches the visible label set, reducing clutter while showing that all three descriptions refer to the same fixed terminal points.

authoredContext:
Now that we have learned how to find the cosine and sine values for special angles in the first quadrant, we can use symmetry and reference angles to fill in cosine and sine values for the rest of the special angles on the unit circle. They are shown in the figure. Take time to learn the (x,y) coordinates of all of the major angles in the first quadrant.

Special angles and coordinates of corresponding points on the unit circle

Graph of unit circle with angles in degrees, angles in radians, and points along the circle inscribed.

In addition to learning the values for special angles, we can use reference angles to find (x,y) coordinates of any point on the unit circle, using what we know of reference angles along with the identities

discrepancies: All 16 label blocks are rendered at a much smaller relative size than in the source (FS=15 inside an 860×610 viewbox that is scaled down), so at inline width the degree/radian/coordinate text is uncomfortably small compared with the source's prominent labels.

Negative coordinates are typeset with the minus sign inside the numerator (−1 over 2, −√3 over 2) whereas the source places the minus sign outside the fraction (−1/2, −√3/2); also the enclosing parentheses do not scale up around the tall fractions as they do in the source.
A grey 'labels: All' status string is printed at the bottom-right of the drawing canvas — extra chrome not present in the source figure.

Radii stroke weights differ slightly from the source: the axis radii are drawn heavier (1.5) than the oblique radii, and the source's uniform thin spokes with a single heavy circle read a little cleaner.
The slider's 0 position maps to 'none' rather than the 0°/360° point, which is slightly counter-intuitive given the figure explicitly labels 0°/360°.
evaluation.notes: Structurally an excellent reproduction of the unit-circle figure (16 spokes, dots, axis arrowheads, red angle text plus black exact coordinates) with rich, genuinely pedagogical interactions (label-set toggle, snapping θ slider, right-triangle/reference-angle overlay, 7-step demo); the main weakness is label typography — everything is noticeably smaller than the source, and negative fractions/parentheses are typeset incorrectly.
action_items: Increase the label font size (e.g. FS ≈ 19–20) and/or tighten the viewbox so the degree/radian/coordinate text is as prominent relative to the circle as in the source and remains readable at inline width.

Render negatives as a minus sign placed before the fraction bar group (−√3/2) instead of inside the numerator, and scale the enclosing parentheses to the full height of the stacked fraction as in the source.
Remove the 'labels: All' status text from the drawing canvas (move it into the control panel if needed) to keep the default state a clean drop-in replacement for the static image.
Make slider value 0 select the 0°/360° point (with a separate 'Clear selection' state) so every special angle including 0/2π is reachable from the slider.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct; the remaining issues are concrete implementation fixes (font size, fraction/parenthesis typesetting, stray canvas text, slider zero mapping).

claude-opus-5.notes: An excellent, near drop-in reproduction of the unit-circle chart with correct 16 radii, dots, red degree/radian and black exact-coordinate labels, backed by genuinely useful interactions (label-set toggle, snapping θ slider, 7-step demo, click-for-right-triangle); only minor weaknesses are tighter-than-source label spacing and small fraction glyphs at inline size.
action_items: Increase vertical separation between adjacent off-axis labels (e.g. nudge 120°/135° and 225°/240°, 300°/315° rows apart by a few px) so they read as clearly separated as in the source.
Bump the base label font (FS) and fraction numerator scale by ~10–15%, or reduce the viewBox width, so stacked √3/2 fractions stay comfortably legible at typical inline widths.
Extend the four axis arrowheads a little past the circle (as in the source) and verify the manual √ overbar aligns with the radical glyph at all sizes.
Move the selection readout card outside the diagram bounds (or make it a caption strip) so it can never sit over the 90°/120° label band at narrow viewports.
